8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":17,"verseId":7,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Action and Fruit","totalVerses":33,"verseData":{"id":"v17_7","number":7,"title":"The Seed-Sprout-Fruit Model of Karmic Continuity","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"As for a continuum, such as the sprout, It comes from a seed. From that arises the fruit. Without a seed, It would not come into being."},"philosophy":{"insight":"The opponent (Sautrāntika) proposes a solution to v.6's dilemma: the seed-sprout-fruit model. The action (seed) ceases but produces a continuum (sprout) that eventually yields the result (fruit). This bridges the temporal gap without requiring the seed to persist permanently.","madhyamaka":"The Sautrāntika proposes the santāna (continuum) model: bīja (seed/action) → santāna (sprout/continuum/karmic trace) → phala (fruit/result). The continuum mediates between the ceased cause and the later effect, avoiding both permanence and annihilation.","quantum":"Sequential quantum processes: an excited atom → emits a photon → the photon is absorbed by another atom. The initial excitation ceases, but its influence propagates through the photon (intermediary/continuum) to produce a distant effect. Chain of causal transmission without permanence.","bridge":"Both the seed-sprout-fruit model and quantum causal chains show influence propagating through intermediaries. Neither the seed nor the excited atom persists — but their influence is carried forward through a medium (sprout/photon) to produce a distant result.","accessible":"Like the postal system: your letter (seed/action) doesn't stay in your hand (permanent) and doesn't vanish (annihilated). Instead, it enters a delivery system (sprout/continuum) that carries it to its destination (fruit/result). The letter changes hands but the message gets through.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, the seed-sprout-fruit model is an accurate description of how karma works. Ultimately, seed, sprout, and fruit are all empty — the model works not because of inherent entities but because of dependent arising.","commonMisconception":"NOT saying the seed-sprout-fruit model is wrong. It's a correct CONVENTIONAL description. The issue is treating seed, sprout, or fruit as INHERENTLY EXISTING entities. As conventional descriptions, they're fine; as inherent entities, they fail (Ch.1)."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Sequential Quantum Causal Transmission","score":65,"strength":"Medium","explanation":"Quantum processes transmit causal influence through intermediaries (photons, virtual particles) without the original state persisting permanently. Like the seed-sprout-fruit chain: influence propagates through intermediaries.","caveat":"Quantum causal chains are physical processes. The seed-sprout-fruit model is a metaphorical/philosophical framework for karma. The parallel is about causal transmission through intermediaries."},"animation":{"visualBridge":"A seed (action) planted → a sprout grows from it (continuum/karmic trace) → the sprout produces fruit (result). The seed is gone but its influence lives on through the sprout. Parallel: excited atom → photon → absorption.","educationalGoal":"User sees the opponent's solution to v.6's dilemma: intermediary continuum bridging the temporal gap between action and result."},"deeperDive":[{"q":"Who proposes this model?","a":"The Sautrāntika school, which posited bīja (seeds) as mental imprints stored in the consciousness stream that carry karmic potential forward. Later, the Yogācāra school developed this into the ālaya-vijñāna (store-consciousness) — a storehouse of karmic seeds.","realLifeExample":"Different software architectures for storing data: Sautrāntika = individual seeds stored in the stream (like individual cookies in a browser). Yogācāra = a dedicated storehouse (like a database server)."},{"q":"What does the \"sprout\" represent in karmic theory?","a":"The intermediate continuum — the stream of mental moments (or karmic traces) that carries the action's causal potential from the moment of acting to the moment of fruition. It's not the original action (seed) and not yet the result (fruit) — it's the bridge.","realLifeExample":"The postal delivery system between sending and receiving a letter. The letter isn't in your hand (seed) or at its destination (fruit) — it's in the delivery system (sprout/continuum)."},{"q":"Does this solve v.6's dilemma?","a":"Partially: it avoids permanence (the seed ceases) and annihilation (the sprout preserves continuity). But it introduces a new question: what is the ontological status of the sprout? If it's inherently existent, it faces the same permanence/cessation dilemma as the seed.","realLifeExample":"Solving one problem by introducing a middleman — but then the middleman needs explaining too. \"Who delivers the mail?\" → \"The postal service\" → \"How does the postal service work?\" The regress continues."},{"q":"How does Nāgārjuna critique this model?","a":"He doesn't reject the conventional description (seed→sprout→fruit). He rejects treating any of the three as INHERENTLY EXISTENT. If the sprout has inherent existence, it faces the same dilemma as the seed (permanent or annihilated?). The solution: all three are empty and dependently arisen.","realLifeExample":"A relay race where Runner A passes the baton to Runner B to Runner C. The model works — but none of the runners have \"inherent runner-essence.\" They're conventionally runners in a dependent process."},{"q":"Why is the seed analogy powerful?","a":"Because it's intuitive and experientially valid: everyone has seen seeds produce sprouts that produce fruits. It captures the key features: temporal gap (seed → ... → fruit), transformation (seed ≠ fruit), and continuity (causal connection). It's a good CONVENTIONAL model.","realLifeExample":"Plant an apple seed → years of growth → apple tree with fruit. The seed is long gone but its influence produced the fruit. This is how karma works conventionally."},{"q":"How does this connect to the Yogācāra school?","a":"Yogācāra expanded the Sautrāntika seed model by proposing the ālaya-vijñāna (store-consciousness) — a foundational consciousness layer that stores all karmic seeds until they ripen. This became the most detailed Buddhist theory of karmic continuity.","deeper":"The seed analogy is perhaps the most successful Buddhist model for karmic continuity. It was adopted and developed by Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and even some Mādhyamika thinkers. Nāgārjuna's critique is not that the model is wrong conventionally — it's that the entities in the model can't be inherently existent. The model works BECAUSE of emptiness (allowing transformation) not despite it."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"What is the seed-sprout-fruit model?","options":["A) A gardening technique","B) Action (seed) ceases but produces a continuum (sprout) that eventually yields the result (fruit).
